06 / WRITING

Notes on the AI landscape.

All posts on LinkedIn ↗

I write on LinkedIn about where AI is heading and what it takes to build with it. Below are my five most-read posts on the subject, by LinkedIn impressions in September 2026, and more to explore.

LINKEDIN · 22 AUG 202677.1K impressions

The most important AI in India isn’t a chatbot. It’s a translator.

Bhashini and NITI Aayog are putting voice-first AI into government services across 22 scheduled languages: speech recognition, IndicTrans2 translation, and speech synthesis. Frontier models get the headlines; this is the layer that decides whether any of it reaches a billion people.

Read on LinkedIn ↗LINKEDIN · 13 JUN 20252.9K impressions

Apple’s “Illusion of Thinking” and the limits of reasoning models

Given the exact solution algorithm, reasoning models still collapsed on hard puzzles. One executed 100+ Tower of Hanoi steps but failed four moves of an unfamiliar river-crossing puzzle: a reality check on memorisation versus generalisation.

Read on LinkedIn ↗LINKEDIN · 05 AUG 20251.1K impressions

gpt-oss: OpenAI’s first open-weight models since GPT-2

120B and 20B models under Apache 2.0, with tool use and MXFP4 quantisation; the smaller one runs in 16 GB of RAM. A welcome pivot, with caveats: text only, and no training-data disclosure.

Read on LinkedIn ↗LINKEDIN · 29 AUG 2026741 impressions

DeepSeek’s harness makes even the agent loop a plugin

Codex and Claude Code build file tools into the harness core. DeepSeek, inspired by Cordis, treats every capability as a plugin, so tools can be swapped at run time without restarting the agent.

Read on LinkedIn ↗LINKEDIN · 21 MAY 2025578 impressions

Google I/O 2025 and the cost of a universal assistant

Gemini 2.5, AI Mode in Search, Project Astra, Veo 3, and Android XR glasses, and the questions they raise about autonomy, privacy, and over-reliance on AI.

Read on LinkedIn ↗

AGENT ARCHITECTURE19 SEP 2026

Jev: a decision engine for what LLMs shouldn’t do

Agents often force LLMs to act as routers and guardrails. Jev scores a finite set of typed choices in parallel instead of generating text, so there is nothing to parse and the output space is bounded.
